t: This is RAAV, Robot As A Verifier.
Give it a prototype and its manual, and a low-cost robot arm tests
every control it can find, then reports what it measured.
Here it is on a centrifuge it has never seen.
First it surveys the panel with one wrist camera,
finds each control, and pins down exactly where it is.
A model reads the manual and drafts a test plan,
and a person approves it before anything moves.
Then the arm runs the plan.
Every press is force-limited, and fixed rules turn each measurement into a verdict.
When the display didn't match the manual, the run stopped, and the plan was amended.
When the lid handle needed a pinch grip the spec rules
out, the robot refused to guess and reported it.
From there, RAAV traces a fault to its part in CAD, proposes a fix for
a person to approve, and tests the new revision with the same plan.
A fix only counts if the score goes up.
Under the hood, RAAV is two systems.
System 1 is the robot: perception, inverse kinematics,
control, force limits and the verdict rules.
System 2 is a frontier model that reads the manual,
plans, recovers from failed steps and diagnoses causes.
Between them is a small set of tools, and none
of them moves a motor or grades a step.
So either side can be swapped: System 2 can be any of four models,
and System 1 the simulator or a real arm, on any appliance.
Vision-language-action models fold all of this into one
network, so each new task needs new demonstrations.
Our split needs a manual instead.
Its limit: a new kind of control still needs a new skill in System 1.
Why does this matter?
Software already has verification, from AI-written proofs to flight code.
Hardware has nothing like it, so failures surface late,
in biosafety labs, spacecraft and prototypes.
Today, RAAV runs on twelve appliance designs in simulation
and a real centrifuge, with its planner in the cloud.
Any lab with a low-cost arm could do the same.
As AI starts designing hardware, every design should
be measured like this before anyone relies on it.
